newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian Socialists defiant in Berisha standoff.
newsitem.headline: Albanian Socialists defiant in Berisha standoff.

text.p: Albania's new Socialist majority raised the stakes in a standoff with President Sali Berisha on Sunday, saying that if he failed to decree the calling of a new parliament they would convene it themselves.
Berisha met leaders of his Democrats and smaller parties on Saturday to discuss when parliament should meet and who should be prime minister, but Socialist leaders refused to meet him.

"The Socialist Party urges President Sali Berisha to issue the decree to convene the People's Assembly in plenary session and tender his resignation as president of the republic," a party statement said.

"If Berisha does not undertake such steps, the Socialist Party and its allies have the political mandate the people gave them in the elections to convene and constitute the new parliament themselves at the right time."

Berisha, whose Democratic Party suffered a resounding defeat in the June 29 elections, has promised to resign once he has "fulfilled his constitutional obligations" but shows no immediate sign of stepping down.

"Sali Berisha has no more political mandate to decide on the future institutions of the Albanian state," the statement said. "After the overwhelming victory of the opposition in the elections, the only act left to Berisha is to issue the decree convening parliament and to present his resignation.

"All the state institutions will be rebuilt by the political forces which won the mandate of the people in the June 29 elections," it said, adding that the Socialists would not negotiate with Berisha on the new government.
Berisha's Socialist party opponents and their coalition allies won a total of 117 seats to the Democrats' 27.
Socialist Party organising secretary Namik Dokle told Reuters that in the Socialists' view Berisha was now just one of parliament's 155 deputies.
"It is not up to him to launch talks on the new government and it is absurd to ask the other parties which won less than two percent about the next prime minister," he said.
The president has indicated that he would prefer interim prime minister Bashkim Fino to stay on as premier rather than Socialist leader Fatos Nano, the party's preferred candidate.

Berisha's Democrats won controversial elections last year, but his government was forced to resign in March at the height of unrest which followed the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid schemes. Much of the country is still ruled by armed gangs.

Diplomats who have urged a new government to get to work say they are concerned that there may be no prime minister to attend a donors' meeting in Rome at the end of July to discuss aid for the shattered country.
